doc.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025

chapter: Time, Creative Music Studio and drumming
title: Elastic approach to time and the Bill Evans trio influence
summary: He credits Evans, Motian and LaFaro with opening up time and explains freedom in playing the form.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I heard you probably in around 1968 or so, with Charles Lloyd. And I’d had a couple of — I’ll call them epiphanies now but that was another one. This was in Rochester in some hall, and I think it was the first time I’d heard drummers and bassists really — I’ll call it playing with the time. Not straight ahead but a little bit of elastic approach to the time.

Well the elastic approach to the time I think I would credit Bill Evans and Paul Motian and Scott LaFaro for that kind of free, open-it-up freedom for each individual to be playing collectively but have an equal input. And so after that “Live at the Village Vanguard” you know it kind of just spread throughout the jazz community. So you know you could break time up. Break it up. And then go into the time later. But for coloring it really opened that up.

Is it possible to feel the time — I’m thinking of Latin music with the clave that is almost always there but sometimes no one’s playing it. So I guess I’m trying to relate that to a jazz situation where everybody’s feeling it but — I can’t quite finish this question but it’s an interesting thing to observe and hear when the time is there but no one is enforcing it regularly.

Well you could call that freedom. Everybody maybe has an option to play the form or play time or not, or play off of the other musicians’ improvisations. So, especially if you’re not playing a composition that’s written. But you can do it in both cases whether you spontaneously compose or with a composition that we make permutations of.
